Q49255: City on Tampa Bay on Florida's Gulf Coast; its metro area includes St. Petersburg and Clearwater.
Grew from Fort Brooke (1824); Ybor City was the world's cigar-making capital around 1900, with Cuban, Spanish and Italian workers.
Known for MacDill Air Force Base and the Busch Gardens theme park.
Q1480013: Metro area in Minnesota around the meeting of the Mississippi, Minnesota and St. Croix rivers, called the 'Twin Cities'.
Minneapolis grew as the flour-milling capital of the world at St. Anthony Falls; Saint Paul is the state capital.
Home of the Mall of America, one of the largest malls in the US.
The murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020 sparked worldwide protests.
Q245023: Taiwan's second-largest city, in the Taichung Basin in central Taiwan.
Planned in the Qing era as the capital of Taiwan Province; laid out by the Japanese in a grid.
Birthplace of bubble tea (Chun Shui Tang teahouse claims it).
Known for its mild climate and the National Taichung Theater by Toyo Ito.
Q57947: River port in Jiangsu on the north bank of the Yangtze, near its mouth, opposite Shanghai.
Called 'China's first modern city' thanks to the industrialist Zhang Jian, who built factories, schools and the first Chinese-run museum here around 1900.
A centre of shipbuilding and textiles; famous for its many centenarians and long-lived people.
Q597: Capital of Portugal on the Tagus estuary; one of the oldest cities in Western Europe.
Starting point of the Age of Discovery: Vasco da Gama sailed from here to India in 1497.
Largely destroyed by the 1755 earthquake and tsunami, then rebuilt in a grid by the Marquis of Pombal.
Known for its hills, yellow trams, Belém Tower, pastéis de nata and fado music.
Q1899: Capital of Ukraine, on the Dnieper River.
Centre of Kievan Rus', the medieval state from which Ukraine, Belarus and Russia trace their origins.
Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra monastery are World Heritage Sites.
Withstood a Russian assault in 2022; its Maidan square was the scene of the 2004 and 2014 revolutions.
Q1533: Capital of Venezuela, in a valley at about 900 m, separated from the Caribbean by the Ávila mountain.
Birthplace of Simón Bolívar, the liberator of much of South America.
Founded in 1567 by the Spanish as Santiago de León de Caracas.
Grew rich with oil in the 20th century; its hillside slums are called barrios.
Q23768: The largest city in Nevada, in the Mojave Desert; famous for casinos and entertainment.
The Las Vegas Strip, with giant themed resorts, lies just outside the city limits.
Founded in 1905 as a railroad town; boomed after Nevada legalised gambling in 1931 and the nearby Hoover Dam was built.
Nicknamed 'Sin City'; hosts big conventions like CES.
Q16554: Capital of Colorado, at the foot of the Rocky Mountains.
Called the 'Mile High City': it lies about one mile (1,609 m) above sea level.
Founded in 1858 during the Pike's Peak Gold Rush.
Gateway to the Rocky Mountain ski resorts.
Q42666: City in Zhejiang south of Hangzhou Bay, a 'water town' with many canals and stone bridges.
Hometown of writer Lu Xun and calligrapher Wang Xizhi's Orchid Pavilion gathering.
Ancient capital of the Yue state; the legendary flood-tamer Yu the Great is said to be buried here.
Q185453: City on the Chenab River in Punjab, Pakistan; one of the oldest cities in Asia.
Called the 'City of Saints' for its many Sufi shrines, like the tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam.
Besieged by Alexander the Great in 326 BC; conquered by Muhammad bin Qasim in 712.
Known for blue glazed pottery and mangoes.
Q3926: South Africa's administrative capital, seat of the executive branch and all foreign embassies.
Founded in 1855 and named after the Voortrekker leader Andries Pretorius.
Known as the 'Jacaranda City' for the thousands of purple jacaranda trees that bloom in spring.
The Union Buildings and the Voortrekker Monument are landmarks.
Q174691: Capital of Shizuoka Prefecture, between Tokyo and Nagoya.
Retirement home of Tokugawa Ieyasu, the first Tokugawa shogun, at Sunpu Castle.
Known for green tea plantations and views of Mount Fuji.
Its neighbour Hamamatsu, the prefecture's largest city, is home to Suzuki, Yamaha and Kawai.
Q83189: Capital of Goiás in central Brazil, a planned city founded in 1933.
Has a large collection of Art Deco buildings.
Known for its parks and green spaces and for sertanejo country music.
The 1987 Goiânia radiation accident with a stolen caesium-137 source was one of the worst ever.
Q202139: Second-largest city of West Bengal, in the coal-mining belt near Jharkhand.
Grew around the Raniganj coalfield and railways; a centre of the steel industry with neighbouring Durgapur and Burnpur.
Q41183: Syria's largest city by urban area, in the north; one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Its old city with the medieval Citadel and covered souqs (some of the largest in the world) is a World Heritage Site.
An important end point of the Silk Road; known for Aleppo soap made with laurel oil.
Heavily destroyed in the Battle of Aleppo (2012–2016) during the Syrian civil war.
Q1094207: The metropolitan municipality of the Pretoria area in northern Gauteng, South Africa.
Created in 2000, centred on Pretoria and including towns such as Centurion and Soshanguve.
Its name comes from Chief Tshwane, an early ruler in the area.
Q51103: Capital of Valle del Cauca, the main city of southwestern Colombia.
Founded in 1536 by Sebastián de Belalcázar.
Called the 'world capital of salsa' for its dance clubs and the World Salsa Festival.
Was the base of the Cali drug cartel in the 1990s.
Q897320: City in eastern Bangladesh, one of the country's oldest municipalities (1868).
Its Titas gas field is the largest natural gas field in Bangladesh.
Known as the hometown of many famous musicians, e.g. Alauddin Khan, teacher of Ravi Shankar.
Q40738: Turkey's fourth city, at the foot of Mount Uludağ (ancient Mount Olympus of Mysia).
The first capital of the Ottoman Empire (from 1326); the early Ottoman sultans' tombs are here.
Called 'Green Bursa' for its parks; a World Heritage Site for the birth of the Ottoman Empire.
Centre of Turkey's car industry; famous for İskender kebab and silk.
Q210493: Port city on the Shandong Peninsula, formerly known as Chefoo.
Its Changyu winery (1892) was China's first industrial wine maker.
Penglai, a district famous for mirages and the legend of the Eight Immortals, belongs to it.
Q118278: Small city in West Bengal near the Bay of Bengal, on the site of ancient Tamralipta.
In ancient times a major port for trade with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, visited by the Chinese monks Faxian and Xuanzang.
Centre of the 1942 Quit India movement, when it declared a short-lived parallel government.
Q189823: Capital of Hainan, China's southernmost province, on the north coast of Hainan Island.
A port city facing the mainland across the Qiongzhou Strait.
Hainan is being developed into a free-trade port with duty-free shopping.
Nearby is the Leiqiong Global Geopark of volcanic craters.
Q1640079: Second city of Sindh, Pakistan, on the Indus about 150 km northeast of Karachi.
Founded in 1768 by the Kalhora ruler Ghulam Shah; capital of Sindh until the British conquest in 1843.
Known for its windcatchers on rooftops, bangles and the Pakka Qila fort.
Named after Hazrat Ali, also known as Haydar.
Q18125: City in North West England, centre of Greater Manchester.
The world's first industrial city: cotton mills earned it the nickname 'Cottonopolis' in the 19th century.
The first passenger railway (to Liverpool, 1830) and the first stored-program computer (1948) are from here.
Home of Manchester United and Manchester City, and of bands like Oasis and Joy Division.
Q10399: City in the hills of West Java, southeast of Bandung.
Called the 'City of a Thousand Pesantren' for its many Islamic boarding schools.
Known for crafts like woven mats, umbrellas (payung geulis) and embroidery.
Mount Galunggung, a volcano that erupted in 1982, is nearby.
Q25282: Port city in central Vietnam, on the coast at the mouth of the Hàn River.
Called Tourane under the French; site of a large US base during the Vietnam War, where US Marines landed in 1965.
Known for its beaches, the Dragon Bridge and the Marble Mountains.
Gateway to Hội An and Huế, both World Heritage Sites.
Q180921: Sudan's second city, on the west bank of the Nile opposite Khartoum.
Capital of the Mahdist state after 1885; the Mahdi's tomb is here.
The 1898 Battle of Omdurman ended Mahdist rule; a young Winston Churchill took part.
Known for its large camel market and Sufi gatherings.
Q7568: City in south-central Java, the only Indonesian region still ruled by a sultan (also its governor).
Served as Indonesia's capital in 1946–48 during the war of independence.
A centre of Javanese culture: batik, gamelan and wayang puppetry.
Gateway to the Borobudur and Prambanan temples; home of Gadjah Mada University.
Q42941: City on the Yamuna River in Uttar Pradesh, once capital of the Mughal Empire.
Home of the Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal — one of the world's most famous buildings.
Agra Fort and nearby Fatehpur Sikri are also World Heritage Sites.
Part of the Golden Triangle tourist route with Delhi and Jaipur.
Q2634: The largest city of southern Italy, on the Bay of Naples beneath the volcano Vesuvius.
Founded by Greeks as Neapolis ('new city'); its historic centre is a World Heritage Site.
Pompeii and Herculaneum, buried by Vesuvius in 79 AD, are nearby.
Q3733: Capital of Guinea, on the Atlantic coast, originally on Tombo Island and the Kaloum Peninsula.
Founded as a French colonial capital in 1890.
A port that exports bauxite (aluminium ore), of which Guinea has the world's largest reserves.
About one in five Guineans live here.
Q209034: Capital of the State of Mexico, about 60 km west of Mexico City.
At about 2,660 m, one of the highest cities in North America.
Known for its chorizo, the covered market and the Cosmovitral, a botanical garden inside stained-glass walls.
The Nevado de Toluca volcano, with crater lakes, is nearby.
Q2066: City at the centre of the Ruhr, Germany's largest urban area.
Was a centre of coal and steel: the Krupp company was based here.
The Zollverein coal mine complex is a World Heritage Site and design museum.
Was European Capital of Culture in 2010 for the Ruhr region.
Q24639: The largest city of British Columbia, on the Pacific between mountains and the sea.
Founded as a sawmill settlement; named after the British captain George Vancouver.
Home of Stanley Park and a big film industry ('Hollywood North').
Hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics; often ranked one of the most liveable cities.
Q1292186: The conurbation around Birmingham and Wolverhampton in central England.
Includes the Black Country, named for the soot of its 19th-century coal mines and ironworks.
A cradle of the Industrial Revolution and of the British car industry.
Q80989: Capital of Madhya Pradesh, called the 'City of Lakes' for its Upper and Lower Lakes.
Ruled by a line of female rulers, the Begums of Bhopal, in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
The 1984 Bhopal gas disaster at a Union Carbide pesticide plant was the world's worst industrial disaster.
The Buddhist stupas of Sanchi and the prehistoric rock shelters of Bhimbetka are nearby.
Q11025: Capital of Central Java and a major port on the north coast of Java.
Has a well-preserved Dutch colonial Old Town (Kota Lama).
Admiral Zheng He is said to have landed here; the Sam Poo Kong temple honours him.
Known for Lawang Sewu ('thousand doors') building and lumpia spring rolls.
Q2460416: Industrial city just north of Dhaka, part of Greater Dhaka.
A hub of the Bangladeshi garment industry, with a large share of the country's clothing factories.
Home of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Safari Park and the Bhawal National Park.
Q1148552: Metro region east of Los Angeles centred on Riverside and San Bernardino.
Once full of citrus groves (Riverside is where the navel orange industry started).
Today a huge logistics hub with giant warehouses for goods arriving at the LA ports.
Includes desert areas like Palm Springs and the Coachella Valley.
Q37951: Capital of Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost large island; Japan's fifth-largest city.
Founded in 1869 with a grid plan modelled on Kyoto; the area was home to the Ainu people.
Hosts the Sapporo Snow Festival with giant snow sculptures.
Hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics; home of Sapporo beer and miso ramen.
Q2256: The UK's second-largest city, in the West Midlands; often called the 'Second City'.
Known as the 'city of a thousand trades' during the Industrial Revolution; James Watt and Matthew Boulton worked here.
Has more miles of canals than Venice.
Home of Cadbury chocolate and the Bullring shopping centre; birthplace of heavy metal (Black Sabbath).
Q10127: City west of Jakarta in Banten, part of the Jakarta metropolitan area.
Home of Soekarno–Hatta International Airport, Jakarta's main airport.
An industrial city with over 1,000 factories.
Next to the planned city of BSD in South Tangerang.
Q363166: City in southern Jiangxi, on the Gan River.
Its Song-dynasty city wall and a 900-year-old underground drainage system (Fushou Gou) still work.
A large Hakka area and a major producer of rare earth metals and navel oranges.
Nearby Ruijin was the capital of the Chinese Soviet Republic, starting point of the Long March.
Q34932: Capital of Queensland on the Brisbane River; Australia's third-largest city.
Founded in 1825 as a penal settlement for repeat offenders.
Known for its subtropical climate, South Bank parklands and nearby Gold Coast beaches.
Q535534: Capital of Inner Mongolia in northern China; the name means 'Blue City' in Mongolian.
Founded in the 16th century by Altan Khan; a centre of Tibetan Buddhism with the Dazhao Temple.
Known for dairy products: home of Yili and Mengniu, China's biggest milk companies.
Has the tomb of Wang Zhaojun, a Han-dynasty consort married to a Xiongnu ruler.
Q3572: Capital of Tunisia, on the Gulf of Tunis.
The ruins of ancient Carthage, rival of Rome, lie in its suburbs.
Its medina, with the Zitouna Mosque, is a World Heritage Site.
Avenue Habib Bourguiba was the centre of the 2011 revolution that started the Arab Spring.
Q38927: City in southwestern Guangdong on the South China Sea.
Grew as a centre of oil shale and oil refining since the 1950s.
Famous for lychees and longans; Gaozhou is a major lychee-growing area.
Hometown of Lady Xian, a 6th-century leader who united the region with the Chinese empire.
Q2900: Capital of Ecuador, at 2,850 m in the Andes — one of the highest capitals in the world.
Its colonial centre is one of the best-preserved in the Americas and was among the first World Heritage Sites (1978).
The equator line (Mitad del Mundo monument) runs just north of the city.
Overlooked by the active Pichincha volcano.
Q975: Home of the Alamo, the mission where Texan defenders were killed by Mexican troops in 1836 ('Remember the Alamo!').
Its five Spanish missions are a World Heritage Site; the River Walk follows the river through downtown.
Known for Tex-Mex food and a majority Hispanic population.
Q38968: Industrial city in Guangxi on the Liu River.
Famous for luosifen, a spicy and smelly river-snail rice noodle soup.
A centre of car-making: SAIC-GM-Wuling builds small cars and vans here.
Known for karst hills around the city; the Tang poet Liu Zongyuan was governor here.
Q43595: Benin's largest city and seat of government, between the Atlantic and Lake Nokoué; the official capital is Porto-Novo.
Its Dantokpa Market is one of the largest open-air markets in West Africa.
Ganvié, a village built on stilts in Lake Nokoué, is nearby.
Its name means 'mouth of the river of death' in Fon.
Q9248: Capital of Azerbaijan on the Caspian Sea; at 28 m below sea level, the lowest-lying capital in the world.
An early centre of the oil industry: around 1900 it produced half of the world's oil.
Its walled old city with the Maiden Tower and the Palace of the Shirvanshahs is a World Heritage Site.
Known for the modern Flame Towers and the Heydar Aliyev Center by Zaha Hadid.
Q1563: Capital of Cuba, on the north coast facing the Florida Straits.
Founded by the Spanish in 1519; for centuries the treasure fleets gathered here before sailing to Spain.
Old Havana and its fortifications are a World Heritage Site; known for 1950s American cars and the Malecón seawall.
Centre of the 1959 revolution of Fidel Castro.
Q93230: City in Punjab, Pakistan, next to Islamabad — together called the 'twin cities'.
Grew as the largest British army garrison town in northern India after 1849.
The ancient Gandhara city of Taxila, a World Heritage Site, is nearby.
Q1255941: Small town on the Ganges in Saran district, Bihar, part of the Patna urban area.
Its name is said to come from 'Dirgh-dwar' (large gate).
Was the seat of a feudal estate under British rule.
Q4789666: City on the Malabar Coast of northern Kerala; formerly called Cannanore.
Known as the land of 'looms and lores' for its handloom weaving and Theyyam ritual dance.
St. Angelo Fort was built by the Portuguese in 1505.
Seat of the Arakkal kingdom, Kerala's only Muslim royal family.
Q12829733: Capital of Pará and gateway to the Amazon, on the Pará River near the Atlantic.
Founded in 1616 by the Portuguese; grew rich in the rubber boom around 1900.
Its Ver-o-Peso market is one of the oldest in Brazil; the Círio de Nazaré procession draws millions.
Hosted the COP30 UN climate conference in 2025.
Q20927: South Korea's fourth-largest city, in a basin in the southeast.
Historically a centre of the Korean herbal medicine trade (Yangnyeongsi market).
Home of Samsung's founding company and of textile industries.
The Haeinsa temple with the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks is nearby.
Q200016: The largest city of Andhra Pradesh, on the Bay of Bengal between the Eastern Ghats and the sea; also called Vizag.
Headquarters of the Indian Navy's Eastern Command and home of large shipyards.
Has a big natural harbour and steel plant.
Known for its beaches like RK Beach and the Araku Valley in the hills nearby.
